[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) data linked to patent and R&D expenditure records for U.S. firms (2000-2020) — This source allows direct estimation of wage growth trajectories for native specialized workers in non-innovating firms (low patenting, low R&D) following the hiring of high-skilled immigrants, controlling for firm and worker fixed effects.

[PATH:empirical] IAB Establishment Panel and Employment Biographies (SIAB) for Germany, matched to firm-level innovation surveys (2000-2020) — Western European data with detailed firm innovation status and worker-level wage histories can test whether the negative wage effect is concentrated in non-innovating firms and in fields with high substitutability.

[PATH:literature] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping' and subsequent refinement by Peri & Sparber (2009) on task specialization — These foundational and counter-argument papers provide the theoretical and empirical framework for substitutability between immigrants and natives, helping to specify the conditions under which wage growth reductions occur.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data on patent filings and wage growth by skill level (e.g., from OECD or Eurostat, 2000-2020) — If high-skilled immigration raises demand for specialized skills, patent counts and wage premiums for native high-skilled workers should increase in advanced economies over the period, providing a direct test of the innovation and demand channel.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of high-skilled visa policy changes (e.g., H-1B cap variations in the US or similar programs in Canada/Australia) on native wages and bargaining outcomes — Such natural experiments can isolate the causal effect of high-skilled immigrant inflows on native workers' wage negotiation power, controlling for confounding factors like overall economic trends.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor market bargaining with endogenous innovation (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2018; Peri & Sparber, 2009) — These models formalize the conditions under which high-skilled immigration enhances native bargaining power via skill complementarity and innovation spillovers; testing their predictions against data can confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Task-based labor market models with endogenous technology adoption (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2018) extended to include immigrant skill flows and firm-level R&D thresholds. — Provides microfoundations for why high R&D intensity amplifies complementarity (innovation tasks) while low R&D leads to routine task overlap, explaining the predicted null/negative effect.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of empirical studies on immigration and native wages focusing on firm heterogeneity, particularly R&D intensity or patenting activity (e.g., Kerr & Lincoln, 2010; Peri et al., 2015). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the conditional effect is supported or contradicted, and identifies gaps in firm-level R&D data usage.

qualifier.tension: Contrasts with uniform complementarity; predicts null or negative effect in low-R&D firms due to routine task overlap.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G.J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1335-1374. — This study uses a cross-city approach to estimate the wage effects of immigrant inflows, directly testing the hypothesis that increased labor supply reduces native bargaining power in specialized occupations.

[PATH:empirical] Peri, G. (2012). 'The Effect of Immigration on Productivity: Evidence from U.S. States.' Review of Economics and Statistics, 94(1), 348-358. — This research examines complementarities between high-skilled immigrants and native workers, offering a counterpoint that increased supply may not always reduce native wage negotiation power if productivity gains offset competition.
